Course Numbers
The BYU AI Foundry is an AI-native product studio and consultancy, and an official program of the BYU Marriott School of Business. We build AI products. One team works out what is worth building and then ships it, because those are no longer two jobs.
This site is the student program guide. It covers the course, how client teams are staffed, and the standard your work is held to. Everything written for prospective clients is on the official website, aifoundry.byu.edu.
The Foundry is not an internship placement and not a research project. Every engagement ends with software running in the client’s hands, and a real company has paid for it.
Build, IS 693R / MSB 341, is the prerequisite. It is offered every fall and every winter. Exceptions are granted for the 2026-2027 school year, since the Foundry is running for the first time and nobody has had the chance to take it yet. See The Builder and the Consultant for the three pathways through this year, the self-assessment, and what the commitment involves.
This course is cross-listed under two course numbers. It is all the same class: everyone meets together Fridays 8:00 to 11:50 AM in 1244 TNRB, works on the same client teams, uses this site, and is graded on the same rubric. Register under whichever number fits your program.
Mixed MBA and undergraduate teams are intentional. The MBAs bring the business judgment, the undergraduate builders bring engineering depth, and on a Foundry team those are the same job.

How We Develop Builders
The Foundry trains full-stack product builders: people who can carry an idea from a user problem to a working product someone actually uses, with AI as both the material and the tool.
Two shapes describe that person.

The Builder is what you can make. Six axes: Discovery, Design, Application Architecture, AI Systems, Agentic Workflow, and Launch and Learn. Students self-report on all six at the start of fall semester and again in December, and see their own profile both times.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
Our principles
Lists of values often list principles to be maximized such as: be excellent, be truthful, be bold. Such lists are helpful but often suffer from two limitations.

Almost any good quality can be taken to excess. Excellence can overshoot into perfectionism. Boldness can overshoot into recklessness. A simple list of values usually provides no way to acknowledge “it’s possible to do too much of a good thing.”
Two good principles may collide with each other. Speed collides with rigor. Candor collides with kindness. Excellence collides with a deadline.

Fortunately, Aristotle elegantly solved both limitations by using a concept he called the Golden Mean. The character traits we seek often sit between two failure modes: doing too little or doing too much. Courage is not the opposite of cowardice; it sits as a Golden Mean, that is, a weighted average, between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity sits between stinginess and waste.
Aristotle was clear that the Golden Mean is not fixed by a formula but rather found by good judgment, and good judgment comes from reflecting on real experience, either your own or that of others.
Aristotle called these qualities virtues. We call them principles, which is more modern language for the same concept. Each of the fourteen below is written with possible failure modes named.
These principles are aspirational and we may frequently miss the Golden Mean. Yet we keep striving, and over time develop true wisdom and good judgment.
We are successful when we can honestly say this of ourselves:

“Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made the effort to become the best of which you are capable.”
John Wooden

section: When there is no golden mean
text:
When there is no golden mean
Aristotle is explicit that the idea of the golden mean has limits: some things “imply by their names that they are themselves bad,” and of those “it is not possible, then, ever to be right with regard to them.”

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
Sometimes principles collide
They will. Rigor says check it again; the deadline says ship. Courage says say it now; discernment says not in this room, not in front of these people. Excellence says raise the bar; patience says this is not the week.
Three things can be helpful when collisions occur:
Name the collision out loud. “I think rigor and the deadline are fighting here” is a faster route to a decision than arguing the merits as though only one principle were in play.
Correct against your own pull. Aristotle’s coaching instruction is that aiming straight at the golden mean undershoots, because your own habit is already bending you. Learn which way you personally miss, then overcorrect. “We shall get into the intermediate state by drawing well away from error, as people do in straightening sticks that are bent.”
The red face test. When a situation is genuinely ambiguous, ask: could I explain this decision to a respected leader without being red in the face? If not, do not do it.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
Three pillars
The AI Foundry is a consultancy and a product studio, with a research lab planned for the future.

Consultancy. Client projects for outside organizations. Client work keeps us grounded in real problems and current with what organizations need, and client fees fund the Foundry.
Product studio. Products the Foundry builds and operates as a service for clients and other customers.
Research lab (future). Research that grows out of what we build and see with clients.

Each faculty member owns a portfolio of clients end to end, from finding them to delivering the work, and advises the teams that serve them. The Foundry grows by adding faculty.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
Client teams
A client team is two builder-consultants: an Engagement Lead, who is a second-year MBA, and an Associate, who is an undergraduate junior or senior. Both build and both consult, and the difference between the roles is small. The Engagement Lead also coordinates: they are the client’s main day-to-day contact, have the final say on sprint priorities, and give work a last review before the client sees it. The client relationship itself belongs to the Project Advisor.
Every team carries two projects: a client project and a Foundry product. Client work comes first. When it slows, the Foundry product keeps the team building, so no one waits on a client.
Each team has a Project Advisor, a faculty member who finds the client, sets the scope and fee, meets with the team every week for sprint review and planning, and holds the standard of the work. The Engagement Success Guide sets out what clients expect and how a team works.
What this means in practice:

Who answers for what. The Project Advisor answers to the client. The Engagement Lead answers to the Project Advisor for the result. Each builder-consultant answers for their own work.
Direct feedback. Teammates give feedback to each other first, in both directions.
Escalation. When an issue cannot be resolved within the team, bring it to your Project Advisor, and then to Professor Murff.
Resetting teams. If a team does not work well together it can be recomposed. This is a normal operating mechanism, not a punishment.

title: Constitution and Operating Model

Enrollment and roles
Every member of a client team enrolls in both sections of the AI Foundry, STRAT 490R and MBA 693R, for 6 credits in all. Your role comes from your program, not your section:

Undergraduates are Associates. They build and consult on the client project and the Foundry product, and each owns one or more workstreams.
Second-year MBAs are Engagement Leads. They do the same work. They are also the client’s main day-to-day contact, decide sprint priorities when the team disagrees, and review work before it goes to the client.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
The Ask First feedback culture
Everyone is empowered to give feedback to anyone at any time, respectfully and directly. More important, our norm is to regularly ask for feedback. Asking removes the awkwardness of unsolicited criticism, signals humility, and puts each of us in control of our own growth. A practical habit: at the end of a project, a meeting, or a deliverable review, ask at least one person “what is one thing I could have done better?” Feedback flows in every direction, including to the faculty advisor. In general, teams should carve out 15 minutes for mutual feedback once every two weeks.
The most useful version of that question, given how Part 1 is written, is directional: which way did I miss? Too little or too much is a far easier thing for a teammate to answer than a rating, and it is the only kind of answer you can act on.

title: Client Service Selection Policy
section: Work that sits outside our mandate
text:
Work that sits outside our mandate
We ensure project fit by considering an organization’s primary business and a particular project’s purpose. In general the following categories fall outside our mandate:

Alcohol, tobacco, nicotine, cannabis, and other drugs of dependence.
Coffee, tea, and similar habit-forming beverages.
Volume growth for controlled substances: sales, script volume, and prescriber targeting.
Gambling: sports betting, prediction markets, gamified retail trading, and casino-mechanic monetization.
Pornography and the commodification of sex, in any form or channel.
High-interest lending: payday, title, and refund anticipation.
Political work: parties, campaigns, candidates, PACs, legislative offices, ballot initiative advocacy, and lobbying on a client’s behalf.
Products marketed on unproven or deceptive claims.
Brands whose public marketing is sexualized, innuendo-forward, profanity-forward, or built on party or intoxication culture, regardless of product category.

If a prospective client or project looks like it touches this list discuss with the faculty advisor before a scoping call.

title: The Builder and the Consultant
text:
Take the self-assessment
To deliver on the aspiration of the AI Foundry, all of us are striving to become AI builder consultants.
An AI builder can build things for themselves. That alone makes a great entrepreneur. Adding the consultant dimension raises the challenge, because now you have to build something great for someone else, which puts real weight on judgment, ownership of the outcome, communication, and collaboration.
Two toolkits describe that person.
The Builder is what you can make. Six axes: Discovery, Design, Application Architecture, AI Systems, Agentic Workflow, and Launch and Learn. You self-report these at the start of fall semester and again in December, and you get your own profile back both times.
The Consultant is what changes when the work belongs to someone else. Four axes: Judgment, Ownership, Communication, and Collaboration. Two are about the work (is it the right work, and does it move) and two are about people (do they understand it, and do they trust you). These are not self-reported. The faculty advisor, your teammates, and your clients rate them against observed behavior at midterm and at the end of each term.
Nobody arrives strong on all ten. Teams are staffed so the team covers every Builder axis even when no single member does.
The baseline survey takes about seven minutes. It is self-report, not a test, and it does not affect your grade. We use it to staff teams so every team covers every skill, and to measure how far the cohort moves by December.
Take the Builder self-assessment →
A 2 is more useful to us than an inflated 4.
Once you have your profile, Resources has curated reading and courses for each axis, plus who to follow.

The commitment. The Lab is an intense course. Plan on 10 hours per week, including the Friday studio block, plus typically another 10 hours in weeks when client demand calls for it. That is what this work actually takes, and it is what a paying client is counting on.

Real work you can point at. Production software running in an organization’s hands, shipped under your name, with a client who will take your call.

I am a student in the BYU AI Foundry, a program that trains AI product
builders: people who can carry an idea from a user problem to a working
product that someone actually uses, with AI as both the material and the tool.

The program tracks six skills, called the Builder axes:

  1. Discovery, what to build and for whom
  2. Design, the surface and the flow
  3. Application Architecture, how the app is structured, shipped, and kept
     safe, including wiring a model in: API calls, retrieval pipelines, cost
     and latency
  4. AI Systems, how the models work and why they behave the way they do:
     neural networks, next-word prediction, pretraining, fine-tuning and
     RLHF, embeddings and RAG, context windows, hallucination
  5. Agentic Workflow, putting AI to work: coding agents, project
     instruction files, memory, skills, hooks, subagents, MCP, reviewing
     code an agent wrote, and building AI into the product with prompts,
     tool use, agent loops, and evals
  6. Launch and Learn, instrumentation, metrics, activation and retention,
     experiments, positioning and pricing

I rated myself 1 to 5 on every axis and got back a six-sided chart of my
profile. I am working on one axis at a time, starting with my weakest.

You are my tutor for Discovery: what to build, and for whom.

First, ask me at most four questions to find out where I actually am. Do not
skip this and do not ask more than four.

Then build me an ordered plan from the sources below, with a rough time
estimate for each step. Read each source yourself before you teach from it.

Sources:
https://www.momtestbook.com/
https://www.producttalk.org/prioritize-opportunities/
https://www.svpg.com/articles/
https://basecamp.com/shapeup
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLe-zy5r0Mk

How to teach me:
- One concept per session, thirty minutes maximum. Say where we stopped.
- After each concept, give me one small exercise against my own project. Not a
  toy example. If I do not have a project yet, help me pick one first.
- Make me explain it back, or show you the work. If I am hand-waving, say so

We are done when I can state a real user problem, the evidence that it is

title: Syllabus
text:
Description
The AI Foundry is an AI-native product studio and consultancy inside the BYU Marriott School of Business. Most of the time you will be on a delivery team for a paying client. The client is paying a fee, retains the intellectual property, and expects professional work. Your grade reflects both the quality of your work and the professionalism with which you do it.
The Foundry builds software. Discovery work comes first, and its purpose is to decide what to build. Every engagement ends with software the client is running.
As at any consulting firm, client work arrives on the clients’ schedule. There will be times when you are not staffed to a client project. In those periods you choose your work from the sprint menu: a studio project, work for the Foundry, or learning, such as the Claude courses or the Product Management book.
Participation is a two-semester sequence, fall and winter.

title: Syllabus

What You Will Work On
Foundry work takes three forms. You will be on one of the first two at any given time, and on the third throughout.
Funded engagements. A client pays a fee, retains the intellectual property, and expects professional delivery. These carry the tightest obligations.
Unfunded engagements. Real outside organizations with real stakes and no fee: nonprofits, university units, early-stage ventures, and mission-driven work the Foundry takes because it is worth doing. The standard of work is identical, and the confidentiality and intellectual property obligations still apply on the terms set for that engagement.
Studio projects. The Foundry cannot seat every builder on an outside engagement at once. When you are not staffed, you build your own product to the same standard, with real users, and ship it. See Studio Projects.
Alongside all three, the Claude courses. Anthropic’s free Claude courses are on the sprint menu as Learn items, and what they teach you to build goes into whatever project you are on. See The Certification Track.
Which form you are on is a matter of staffing and timing rather than merit, and it can change between terms. How client teams are set up is in the Engagement Success Guide.

Laptops are the tool. This is a build studio, so laptops are open and expected. The obligation that comes with that is attention: if you are in a client call or a critique, you are in it.

title: Syllabus
text:
Confidentiality and Client Data
Foundry clients share confidential business information: financials, pipelines, customer data, and strategy. This is a condition of the work, and it carries obligations.

You will sign the client’s NDA, or the Foundry’s standard mutual NDA, before receiving data.
Client data stays in the approved project repository and approved tools. It does not go into personal accounts, personal cloud storage, or unapproved AI services.
Nothing about the project goes on LinkedIn, in a portfolio, or in a job interview without written client permission. Ask the faculty advisor first, every time.
Deliverables and intellectual property belong to the client, not to you and not to BYU.
When the project ends, you delete local copies of client data.

A confidentiality breach is an Honor Code matter and will also end the engagement. Treat this as the professional obligation it is.

title: Syllabus
text:
AI Use Policy
You are expected to use AI tools extensively. That is the point of the Foundry. The obligations that come with it:

You own the output. “The model produced it” is not a defense for a wrong number, a fabricated citation, or an analysis you cannot explain.
Every deliverable must be explainable. If you cannot walk the client through why the model recommends what it recommends, it is not done.
Client data goes only into approved tools. See the confidentiality section above.
Disclose your method. Project documentation and your sprint reviews should say what tools and models you used and how you validated the output.

# Sprint N Plan

**Menu:** Build, Learn, or both. For each Build, who it's for: a client
(name it), the Foundry, or your own product. For each Learn, the course
or chapters.

**Teammates:** Who else is working on it, or "Solo."

Did you hit the goal? Yes, partly, or no, and why.
What did the client or your users say or do about the work? For a Learn-only sprint, who did you show it to, and what did they say?
What did the report show you that you did not expect?
If the plan changed, why?
Actual difficulty, 1 to 5, and why it differed from what you predicted.
What will you change next sprint?

title: The Certification Track
text:
Why this certification
The Foundry wants its builders to be able to earn the Claude Certified Developer, Foundations credential. The preparation courses are free, and they are on the sprint menu as Learn items. The exam is optional.
Client work is unpredictable and does not exercise every skill on schedule. These courses do.
The Foundry is a member of the Claude Partner Network. Three of Anthropic’s four certifications count toward the network’s tier requirements, and Developer, Foundations is the one written for the work our builders actually do: engineers who build with the Claude API, Claude Code, and Model Context Protocol, from first integration to production agents.
It is also the most efficient of the three. Same price as Architect, Foundations, same value toward the Foundry’s standing, and four courses of preparation instead of seven.
Registration requires a Foundry email address. Personal addresses will not work. Sitting the exam requires a valid, unexpired government-issued ID whose name matches your registration.

The split is deliberate. The learning is inside our control, so it is required. The exam depends on a third party’s scheduling, proctoring, and pricing, none of which the Foundry controls, so it does not gate your grade.

title: The Certification Track
section: What the exam does not cover
text:
What the exam does not cover
Anthropic’s own description of the Developer certification stops at building. It does not test engagement economics, client communication, responsible deployment, or how to decide whether a thing is worth building at all.
That is the part of the curriculum the Foundry teaches. The certification shows you can build on Claude. It does not test judgment about what to build. List it on a résumé as a building credential.

title: The Certification Track
text:
For the Foundry
The Foundry needs ten active certified builders to reach Select tier in the Claude Partner Network, alongside two client engagements deployed to production and one published customer story. Select is the first tier that appears in Anthropic’s public partner directory.
Certifications expire after 12 months, so this is a standing annual target rather than a one-time push. The target is ten passes each year.

title: Practice Proficiency Exam
text:
A practice exam on what every Foundry builder should know: the six builder axes, taught in the MSB 341 Product Management book. It follows the same plan as the MSB 341 final: the same six axes in the same proportions, and a short case on each axis. No question here appears on the final.
On every question you also mark how sure you are, from 1 (guessing) to 3 (certain). It is never scored. Your results show how often you were right at each level, and they list the questions you were certain about and got wrong first, because those are the ideas that feel settled but are not.
Every explanation links to the section of the Product Management book it comes from. Your answers stay in your browser and are not sent to anyone. The final gives 2 hours for 84 questions; to practice at that pace, allow about 85 minutes.
Start the practice exam

title: Studio Projects
text:
A studio project is real work
Not every builder is on a client engagement at any given moment. The cohort has more builders than there are seats on client engagements, so some builders are always unstaffed. Being unstaffed says nothing about merit.
If you are not staffed, you are on a studio project. It is the same work held to the same standard, without a client paying for it.
A studio project is a real product with real users, built to the Build Standards that govern client work. It ships. On the sprint menu it is a Build for your own product, planned, reviewed, demoed, and graded exactly like client work. The only difference is that no client pays for it.
It matters for three reasons.
It is how you get staffed. Engagements are staffed by reputation, and reputation comes from work people have seen. A shipped studio project, with sprint reviews and demos behind it, is the strongest evidence you can offer that you can do a kind of work you have not done for a client yet.
It is how the Foundry can take on engagements. The Foundry can only take an engagement when it has more than one builder who can do that kind of work. Studio projects are where builders get that experience.
It is where you can practice what a Claude course teaches. Client work is unpredictable and will not use every skill on a schedule. A studio project is yours to shape, so you can deliberately build the thing a Claude course teaches, an evaluation harness, an MCP server, a Skill, and count it as a Learn item in the same sprint. See The Certification Track.

title: The Developmentship Model
text:
The anchors
Developmentship is the individual instrument in this course and the largest single component of your grade, worth 180 of 500 points. This page is the whole model: what it measures, who rates you, how several reviewers become one number, and how that number becomes points.
It scores the four Consultant axes: Judgment, Ownership, Communication, and Collaboration. These are what changes when the work belongs to someone else. See The Builder and the Consultant for how the Consultant diamond sits alongside the Builder hexagon.
Two axes are about the work: Judgment asks whether it is the right work, and Ownership asks whether it moves. Two are about people, and they follow the guiding question for Create Impact with People, “Do people understand, trust, and act on this work?” Communication is the understand half, judged on what you write. Collaboration is the trust half, judged on the relationship with everyone you work with, teammates and the client alike.
The same 1 to 5 scale applies on every axis. There are no adjectives like “strong” or “excellent.” Every level is something a reviewer could point at in a week of work, which is what makes two different reviewers land in the same place.

title: The Developmentship Model
text:
Judgment







1
Solves the problem as handed over, even when it is the wrong one. Conclusions run ahead of the evidence.


2
Sound on the task in front of them, but does not ask whether it is the right task. Reports what the data says, not what it means.


3
Checks that the question is the right one before starting. Conclusions follow from the evidence, and they say where it is thin.


4
Reframes the problem when the facts call for it. Separates what is known from what is assumed; recommendations hold up when tested.


5
The team or client changes direction because of how they framed it. Says what the facts support when it is not what anyone hoped.





Ownership







1
Waits to be told. Work stops when the next step is unclear. Blockers surface at the deadline rather than before it.


2
Does assigned tasks well but does not extend past them. Asks what to do next rather than proposing it.


3
Owns a defined piece and finishes it. Raises blockers early. Still needs the plan handed to them.


4
Owns a workstream end to end. Makes the plan, unblocks themselves, and reports what they decided rather than asking what to do.


5
Owns a workstream and pulls others along. Reprioritizes when the client changes direction, and what comes back is better than what was asked for.





Communication







1
Updates are late or absent. The reader has to ask what happened.


2
Reports activity in the order it happened. The reader has to extract the point themselves.


3
Answer first, support underneath. Someone who reads only the first line knows the state of the work.


4
Writes for the specific reader. Names the decision being asked for, and the memo or deck holds up without anyone narrating it.


5
Produces the artifact the team reuses. A senior stakeholder can act on it without a meeting.





Collaboration
How your teammates and your client experience working with you, over the whole engagement. A student can be quiet in a client meeting and still rate a 4 if the client relies on them between meetings.







1
Works alone; the team and the client find out late. Takes feedback as criticism, or agrees and changes nothing.


2
Does their own part and reacts when asked. Leaves teammates’ work and the client relationship to others; applies feedback only where told.


3
Reliable to work with. Keeps commitments to teammates and the client, shares context without being chased, and acts on feedback the next time.


4
Makes the people around them better. Asks for feedback before it is offered, says early what will not fit, and teammates and the client come to them directly.


5
People ask to work with them again, by name. Handles disagreement without it becoming personal, changes position when someone else is right, and surfaces a risk before anyone else finds it.

text:
The principles are not a fifth axis
There is no values score. Every reviewer is asked one optional question instead: which principle from the Constitution did they see you live, and what did you do? It is positive only. No form in this course asks anyone which principle you failed, because a principle is not something you rate on a scale, and rating each other’s adherence to values is not an instrument we are going to build.
The citations are not scored. They come back to you in your development summary, in your reviewers’ own words, and they tell the Foundry which of its principles are actually visible in the work.
Failures of principle do not travel through a survey. They are raised directly, and the serious ones are conduct matters that leave this model entirely.

title: Engagement Success Guide
text:
Your team
Clients hire the Foundry with high expectations. This guide exists to help teams meet and exceed those expectations, from the first week to roll-off.
Clients have the same AI tools we do. They are looking for expertise, critical thinking and good judgment beyond what they get from AI tools and coding agents alone. Read this guide before your first client call, and refer to the checklist often.
Each client team has three people: a Faculty Project Advisor (Professor Murff or Professor Toborg), an MBA Engagement Lead and an undergraduate Associate. Top-tier consulting firms staff engagements this way because the structure supports coaching, mentorship and growth at every level. To deliver excellent work consistently, the Foundry operates the same way.
Your Project Advisor works closely with your team: solving problems with you and reviewing deliverables before they reach the client. They meet with each team for 25 minutes in the Thursday 9:30 to 10:45 slot, meet at other times as needed, and frequently join client calls.
Because AI lets everyone build, both students build and consult. The Engagement Lead’s coordination is added to their build work.
Both of you:
Leading client engagements. In a consulting firm, the engagement lead has typically been an associate first. Most Engagement Leads in the Foundry have not, so taking the lead may be a gradual transition from the Project Advisor. Early on, your Project Advisor may lead client meetings with the Engagement Lead alongside. As the Engagement Lead demonstrates they are ready, they begin to lead meetings, and the Project Advisor continues to join calls where helpful.
Both the Engagement Lead and the Associate spend 20 hours a week on the team’s work.

Name owners. Unowned priorities do not get done.
Ask for what you need explicitly. Clients do not know what you need unless you tell them, and you are responsible for any blocker you did not raise.
Flag risk early and unemotionally. A risk raised in week 4 can still be planned around. Raised in week 12, it usually cannot.
Be concise. Bullets, not paragraphs.
Never pad. A short honest week is fine. A long week of activity with no outcomes is not.

title: Build Standards
text:
The Four Dimensions
Client work you submit as sprint output is read against these standards. They are also what separates work a client pays for from work a client tolerates.
Every deliverable is scored on correctness, usefulness, explainability, and craft.

title: Build Standards
text:
Correctness

Code does what it claims. If it is shipped, it has been run against something real
Every number in a client-facing document traces to a source you can point to
Totals reconcile. If your revenue baseline is 2% off the client’s actuals, you find out why before you present it, not after they do
Assumptions are written down as assumptions, with the value used and the reason for it
If you do not know something, the deliverable says so. Fabricated precision is worse than an honest range



Usefulness

Someone at the client would actually open it. A tool nobody uses is a failed deliverable
It solves the problem the client actually has, integrated with the systems they actually run
Discovery output names specific things to build, with an estimate and a sequence, not themes
Scope creep is not usefulness. If the client’s question changed, renegotiate it in writing



Explainability
This is the standard the Foundry is built around, and it is where AI-assisted work most often fails.

For any model output, you can state which inputs drove it and by how much
Rankings come with sensitivity: what would have to change for the order to change
A model no one on the team can explain is not shippable, regardless of how good the output looks
“The model said so” is never an answer to a client question



Craft

The repository is clean, has a README, and someone outside the team could run it
Tests exist where breakage would be expensive. Not everywhere, but not nowhere
Deployment is documented and repeatable, not a thing one person knows how to do
Documents are proofread. Charts are labeled. Slides have a point per slide
No client data in personal accounts, personal repos, or unapproved tools

title: Build Standards
text:
Repository Standards
Every engagement has one private repository in the ai-foundry-byu GitHub organization, named client-<slug>.
client-<slug>/
  README.md          What this is, how to run it, how to deploy it, who to ask
  discovery/         The audit: findings, what to build, estimates, sequence
  app/               The application. Whatever stack the job calls for
  integrations/      Connections into the client's systems
  analysis/          Notebooks and scripts, in order, that reproduce every number
  deliverables/      What the client actually receives, versioned by delivery
  docs/              Handoff docs, meeting notes, decision log, scope changes
Two rules that are not negotiable:

No secrets or client data in the repository. Ever. Credentials live in the client’s own systems or an approved secret store.
Every number in a deliverable is reproducible from something in analysis/. If you cannot rerun it, you cannot defend it.

title: Build Standards
text:
The Decision Log
Keep docs/decisions.md current. One entry per material decision:
2026-10-09: Price erosion assumption
Decision: Use 12% annual erosion for specialty, 18% for hospital, rather than a
flat 15% across the portfolio.
Why: Client's 2023-2025 actuals show materially different curves by channel.
Who: Confirmed with Brian Guy on the Oct 8 call.
Reversible: Yes. Sensitivity range 8-22% is built into the model.
This is the single highest-leverage habit in the course. It is what lets you answer “why did you assume that” six months later, and it is what makes handoff possible.

title: Build Standards
text:
QC Gate
Nothing goes to the client without the QC lead’s sign-off. The QC lead checks:

It runs. Someone other than the author has run it from a clean checkout
Every number traces to a source, and totals reconcile against the client’s own figures
Assumptions are stated, with values and reasons
Model outputs are explainable in plain language
Deployment steps are written down and have been followed once by someone else
No client data or secrets in the repository
Document is proofread, charts are labeled, filenames are clean

Work that fails QC after it reaches the client is a miss for the whole team, and the client notices it. Catch it internally.

title: Build Standards
text:
Working with AI
Use AI tools hard. They are why a team of five can deliver what used to take fifteen.

Generate freely, verify always. Treat every model output as a draft from a fast, capable, occasionally confident-and-wrong analyst.
Check citations and figures by hand. Fabricated sources have ended real consulting engagements.
Keep client data out of unapproved tools. See the confidentiality terms in the Syllabus.
Document your method. Project documentation and your sprint reviews should state which tools you used, for what, and how you validated the output. This is not a confession, it is methodology.
